query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating an optimal amount of tungsten (approximately 0.5 at.%) into an AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will reduce both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide temperature range by promoting the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds and facilitating a protective, lubricious oxide film during service.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated AlCoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with a microstructure lacking tungsten-induced phases and with moderate tribological performance under sliding wear conditions.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base high‐entropy alloy with tungsten to form an alloy composition around AlCoCrFeNiW0.5.
generation.conditions: Service conditions covering a broad temperature range (from room temperature up to ~900°C) under sliding wear conditions with standard loads encountered in self-lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: The introduction of tungsten leads to the formation of finely dispersed W-rich intermetallic compounds within a BCC phase and induces notable lattice distortion, both of which support enhanced load-bearing and promote controlled oxide layer development.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten alloying increases hardness and load-carrying capacity while triggering the formation of a stable lubricious oxide layer during frictional contact. This dual effect reduces friction fluctuations and wear loss even under elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the tungsten-alloyed high-entropy alloy is expected to show a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and a significantly reduced wear rate under similar loading and temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy that typically exhibits higher friction coefficients and wear rates due to less effective oxide layer formation and lower inherent hardness.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only at optimal tungsten levels (~0.5 at.%); deviations (e.g., excessive tungsten) could lead to undesirable phase formation or mechanical brittleness. The intervention may not be effective under extreme loads or environmental conditions outside the tested temperature range.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative improvements are anticipated, the precise quantitative changes in friction coefficient and wear rate are uncertain until validated by systematic experiments. The interplay between tungsten-induced intermetallic formation and oxide layer behavior under varying sliding speeds also remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the untreated AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy and one alloyed with ~0.5 at.% tungsten (AlCoCrFeNiW0.5). Process both sets using the same fabrication method (e.g., laser cladding or spark plasma sintering) to ensure similar microstructures except for the tungsten addition. Conduct standardized sliding wear tests at multiple temperatures from room temperature to ~900°C under the same load and sliding speed conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (measured by mass loss or volume loss)
Microstructural analysis to verify the formation and distribution of W-rich intermetallic compounds and oxide layers (using SEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-alloyed samples do not consistently show lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates across the test temperature range compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Investigating the tribological characteristics of copper surface composites reinforced with high entropy alloy (AlCoCrCuFe) through friction stir processing

Abstract: AbstractThe present investigation focuses on the fabrication of Copper-High Entropy Alloy (HEA) surface Metal Matrix Composite (MMC) using the solid-state Friction Stir Process (FSP) and the characterization of wear characteristics. Higher hardness values at the level of 770HV were the cornerstone in its selection, in addition to identifying several appropriate considerations for combining the AlCoCrCuFe HEA in Cu-HEA surface MMCs. Because of the combination of FSP and HEA, the produced composite had a fine microstructure and increased hardness. The wear test is carried out using pin-on-disc equipment for all conceivable parameter combinations to thoroughly analyze wear qualities, with velocity, load, as well as sliding distance chosen as input parameters. The wear rate decreases dramatically with HEA additions and rises with sliding velocity, load, and sliding distance. Effects of W Alloying on the Lattice Distortion and Wear Behavior of Laser Cladding AlCoCrFeNiWx High-Entropy Alloy Coatings

Abstract: AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation.
